comparator.name: Dutch Languages and Cultures — Dutch Language and Culture
comparator.sourceNotes: This is the Dutch Language and Culture track for September 2026 entrants. The second- and third-year courses in these regulations begin in 2027–2028 and 2028–2029.
components: Complete workshops in two different areas chosen from literature, linguistics and language use.
Before starting, complete at least 50 EC from year one, earn at least 100 EC in the degree overall, and pass Research Approaches.

routeSelection.basis: The University of Groningen regulation distinguishes Dutch Language and Culture and Frisian Language and Culture. The normalized registry target itself names Dutch Language and Culture, so this formal route is selected before and independently of evaluating any UCR course fit. The route's genuine 30-EC minor remains open rather than being populated with an invented specialization.

audience.programmeDescription: Students study Dutch literature from the Middle Ages to the present and examine the structure, history and use of Dutch. They apply these methods in research workshops and a thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR combination studies how texts create meaning and how people argue, write and use language, combining literary interpretation, stylistics, rhetoric and psycholinguistics. Groningen develops those subjects specifically through Dutch literary history, language structure and advanced use of Dutch.

core: Dutch-language literature from the Middle Ages to the present, literary interpretation, creative writing and the relationship between literature and society
Dutch language structure, change, meaning, variation, rhetoric, writing and public communication
Language acquisition, cognition and critical analysis of digital communication
Dutch culture, social identity, mediated narratives and contemporary social questions
Qualitative, literary, linguistic and statistical methods culminating in a Dutch Studies thesis
adjacent: Language, cognition and public communication: acquisition, variation, persuasion, debate and digital discourse
Literature, writing and culture: historical texts, creative practice, performance, society and mediated identity
Digital and empirical methods for studying language, texts and communication
questions: How do language, rhetoric and media shape identity, politics and public debate?
How do literary texts and stories interpret society across historical periods and media?
How do narratives and mediated identities connect literature, cultural memory and contemporary society?

alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest response, six courses (45 EC) replace psycholinguistics, statistics, programming, data science and advanced historical research with media archaeology, environmental media, documentary and denser art-historical study. It differs by ten courses (75 EC) from the language-and-digital-society route.

trace: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project.
Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data.
Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity.
Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality.
Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline.
Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination.
Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language.
Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes.
Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice.
Develops beginner Dutch for everyday oral and written communication while introducing Dutch culture.
Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction.
Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work.
Studies and develops creative communication through poetry, performance and critically articulated artistic practice.
Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice.
Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception.
This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present.
Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation.
Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization.
Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty.
Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation.
Studies the translation of literary narratives into film through formal analysis and adaptation theory.
Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation.
Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance.
Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks.
Examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media.
Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations.
Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture.
Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production.
